Data Appreciation · Week 7 · Title

Reading charts critically: how charts mislead

A chart can be accurate and still mislead — through a cut axis, a cherry-picked range, 3-D effects or a missing source.

Next Generation Genius · Year 1 · Foundation

Data Appreciation · Week 7 · Goals

By the end of today

  • Spot four common tricks in charts
  • Explain how a truncated axis exaggerates
  • Rewrite a misleading chart honestly
Data Appreciation · Week 7 · Idea 1

Understand it

Four tricks to look for:

  1. Truncated axis — the bar chart starts at 95, not 0, so 96 and 98 look wildly different. Bar charts must start at zero.
  2. Cherry-picked range — showing only the weeks that went up.
  3. 3-D and pictures — slices or icons drawn bigger than their numbers.
  4. No source, no date, no units — you cannot check it.

Before you believe a chart, ask: *What is the axis? What is missing? Who made it, and why?* A line chart may start above zero if the change is the point — but it must say so.

Data Appreciation · Week 7 · Key words

Key words

Truncated axis
an axis that does not start at zero
Cherry-picking
showing only the data that supports a claim
Source
where the data came from
Data Appreciation · Week 7 · Practice

Now you do it

  1. Look at the same data drawn two ways
  2. Hunt for the trick in five real charts
  3. Redraw one honestly

Need a hand? Use the checklist: axis from zero? whole time range? source? units?

Done early? Make a chart that is technically correct but misleading on purpose, then fix it — and explain the difference.

Data Appreciation · Week 7 · Assessment

How you will be assessed

  • A bar chart of attendance has its axis starting at 95%. Monday is 96%, Tuesday 98%. What does the chart wrongly suggest?
  • Name two questions to ask before you believe a chart in an advert.
  • Bring one misleading chart you found; show your instructor the trick and your honest redraw.

Your work is marked against the rubric, and you may be asked to explain your choices. Show your own thinking.
